text: Proof. By Theorem 5.4(3) a counterexample \(Q\) of least order has order \(3^8\) or \(3^9\), and Lemma 6.2 applies to it; for order \(3^9\) we may use the result for order \(3^8\). The deduction for \(G\) is as in Theorem 5.4.

Order \(3^8\). Every group is in the SmallGroups library (package sglppow [VLE]). Of the \(1\,396\,077\) groups, \(904\) are non-metabelian of class \(4\); all have rank \(3\) (as they must, Proposition 6.5), \(|Z|=|Q''|=|\gamma_4|=3\) and \(Q/\gamma_2\cong C_3^3\), types \((3,2,2,1)\) (\(889\)) and \((3,3,1,1)\) (\(15\)), by a computation over the library. So Theorem 6.6 gives \(D_5=1\) for all of them. Independently, \(699\) of them have \(z\in Q''\cap M_5\), and for each the truncated Magnus algebra (\(121\) monomials, modulo \(3^{19}\), with the exactness certificate \(3^{18}\Delta\subseteq\Delta^5+3^{19}\)) gives \(z\notin D_5\).

Order \(3^9\). Let \(Q\) be a counterexample and \(P=Q/\langle zangle\), of order \(3^8\) and class \(3\) or \(4\). By Proposition 6.5(2), \(d(Q)\in\{3,4\}\); the case \(d(Q)=5\), type \((5,2,1,1)\), is excluded by hand (alternatively, by Theorem 6.15: all \(7\,824\) possible parents are rejected by Lemma 6.14, as a full run confirms). For \(d\in\{3,4\}\) we use computation: of the \(771\,597\) groups \(P\) of order \(3^8\), rank \(3\) or \(4\) and class \(3\) or \(4\), \(3\,986\) pass the filter of Lemma 6.14; ANUPQ lists their \(305\,583\) immediate descendants of step size \(1\); \(64\,362\) have class \(4\), \(Q''
e1\) and cyclic centre, and \(62\,245\) of these have \(z\in Q''\cap M_5\). For each of the \(62\,245\) the truncated Magnus algebra gives \(z
otin D_5\), exactly. The presentations given to it were checked independently with ANUPQ (order \(3^9\), class \(4\), \(z\) central of order \(3\) in \(Q''\cap M_5\)). The filter was validated against full expansion on a range and a random sample of \(1500\) parents, without loss of a candidate. The descendant step was repeated with an ANUPQ in which the defects found in an audit of the package are fixed (https://ispacex.github.io/gap/; two of them give wrong descendants for inputs not met here): for each of the \(3\,986\) parents the numbers of descendants, of groups of class \(4\) with \(Q''
e1\) and cyclic centre, and of candidates are the same, and the \(62\,245\) presentations are identical.
Cost and data. The order-\(3^9\) run took \(3\) h \(21\) min on \(4\) cores; the filter cut the time per parent from about \(350\) to \(27\) ms. Code: compute/magnus.

e1\) and order \(\ge2^{12}\) (Proposition 5.10); at order \(2^{12}\) it is a candidate of rank \(\le8\) (after Proposition 5.10). By Tahara [Tah77a, Cor. 18 and 21] a counterexample has \(d(Q)\ge4\) (Remark 5.11). Already \(D_4
e\gamma_4\) needs order \(\ge2^{11}\) (§5, after the sections of Rips's group), while the smallest known example, Rips's group, has order \(2^{38}\). Using the truncated Magnus algebra (\(\mathbb{Z}[G]/\Delta^n\cong T_{<n}(\mathbb{Z}^k)/I_n\) for a \(k\)-generator presentation, of rank \((k^n-1)/(k-1)\) independent of \(|G|\)) we checked the class-\(3\) quotients of the three-relator Rips-type group of [BM23, §1.2] and of \(13\) variants (orders \(2^{40}\)–\(2^{107}\)): \(D_5=1\) in all of them, including three, of orders \(2^{84}\), \(2^{90}\) and \(2^{107}\), with \(D_4
e1\). Two independent implementations agree on these results, and the exactness certificate holds in all cases, so \(D_4
e1\) and \(D_5=1\) are proved, not only modulo \(2^{30}\). The method (code: https://gitlab.com/ispacex/cflint-core) was also checked against the lattice computation on \(30\,435\) groups of order \(\le 3^7\) without discrepancies, and is \(200\)–\(400\) times faster at order \(3^7\). • Is there \(3\)-torsion in \(D_5(G)/\gamma_5(G)\) for some \(G\), i.e. is Tahara's bound \(6\) attained? (“Rips's abyss” in Mikhailov's talk [Mik13].) Tahara expected the bound \(6\) to be the best one [Tah81, p. 142]. At the end of the paper he announced a separate paper [Tah81, p. 173], which would show \(D_5(G)=\gamma_5(G)=1\) for his \(2\)-groups with \(D_4
e\gamma_4\) [Tah77b] and construct counterexamples to \(D_5(G)=\gamma_5(G)\). The announcement does not say that their quotient \(D_5/\gamma_5\) would have \(3\)-torsion, and \(D_5
e\gamma_5\) with \(2\)-torsion is known anyway: \(2\mid s(5)\) in the notation of [BM23, §1]. We have not been able to locate this paper (the conference report [THSH81] of 1981 is on other topics), and we could not obtain his surveys in Bull. Aichi Univ. Educ. (1981, 1982). According to its zbMATH review, Tahara's survey of 2003 [Tah03] reports Gupta's claim that the exponent of \(D_n/\gamma_n\) is at most \(2\). Bartholdi and Mikhailov [BM23, §1] state the bound as \(s(5)\in\{2,6\}\), i.e. open. By the results of this paper, there is no \(3\)-torsion when the Sylow \(3\)-subgroup has order \(\le3^9\) (in \(D_n/\gamma_n\) for every \(n\), see below), and \(D_5=\gamma_5\) when \(G/\gamma_2\) is a finite \(3\)-group and \(\gamma_2/\gamma_3\) has exponent \(3\) (Theorem 6.9), or, more generally, \(\gamma_4^3\subseteq\gamma_5\) (Theorem 6.11, which contains Theorem 6.10); by [Gup91] a finite metabelian group has no \(3\)-torsion in \(D_n/\gamma_n\), so an example must be non-metabelian. A minimal \(3\)-group with \(D_5
e\gamma_5\) has order \(\ge3^{10}\), class \(4\), cyclic centre, \(\gamma_2/\gamma_3\) of exponent \(\ge9\) (hence at least two invariants \(\ge9\) in \(Q/\gamma_2\)), and \(\gamma_4\le Z(Q)\) cyclic of order \(3^k\) with \(k\ge2\), with \(D_5(Q)=\Omega_1(\gamma_4)\) (Corollary 6.12 and the paragraph after it), so \(\gamma_4\cong C_9\) when the second largest invariant of \(Q/\gamma_2\) is \(9\) (Theorem 6.9 and the paragraph after it). Open is the case \(\gamma_4^3
ot\subseteq\gamma_5\), that is, for a minimal \(Q\), \(\gamma_4\) cyclic of order \(\ge9\). Already for \(\gamma_4\cong C_9\) the identity \((\star)\) of the proof of Theorem 6.11 holds, but its terms are only known to lie in \(\gamma_4^3\) (Remark 6.13); by computation, \(D_5=1\) in \(940\) random groups with \(\gamma_4\cong C_9\) and cyclic centre. For every \(n\), a \(3\)-group with \(D_n
e\gamma_n\) has order \(\ge3^{10}\); the smallest known example, a quotient of the Bartholdi–Mikhailov group, has order \(3^{493}\) (§5). Let \(Q\) be a \(3\)-group of least order with \(D_n
e\gamma_n\). Then \(\gamma_n(Q)=1\) (pass to \(Q/\gamma_n\)), so \(Q\) has class \(c<n\). Every proper quotient has \(D_n=\gamma_n=1\), so \(D_n(Q)
e1\) lies in every nontrivial normal subgroup; hence the centre is cyclic and its socle \(\langle zangle=D_n(Q)\) lies in \(D_{c+1}(Q)\), in the Jennings subgroup \(M_{c+1}(Q)\) and, by [Gup91] applied to \(Q/Q''\), in \(Q''\). Class \(\le3\) is impossible (\(D_4=\gamma_4\) in a \(3\)-group [Pas68]), and class \(4\) gives \(D_n\subseteq D_5=\gamma_5=1\) by Theorem 6.19. Of the groups of order \(3^6\), \(3^7\), \(3^8\) of class \(\ge5\), \(1035\) satisfy these conditions, and all have \(z
otin D_{c+1}\), by an exact computation in the truncated Magnus algebra (code: compute/magnus). At order \(3^9\) a least-order \(Q\) of class \(\ge5\) is an immediate descendant of step size \(1\) of \(P=Q/\langle zangle\), since the last term of its lower exponent-\(3\) central series is nontrivial, central and of exponent \(3\), hence lies in \(\Omega_1(Z(Q))=\langle zangle\) and equals it; \(P\) has class \(\ge c-1\ge4\) and rank \(d(Q)\le5\), as \(d(Q)+c-1\le9\). Of the \(66\,569\) such \(P\), \(4\,627\) pass a necessary test on the \(p\)-cover (with \(Q=P^*/U\), each of \(z\in Q''\), \(z\in M_6(Q)\), \(\gamma_5(Q)
e1\) requires a subgroup of the multiplier not contained in \(U\), and so does \(Q\) being a descendant: the nucleus is not in \(U\)); ANUPQ lists their \(65\,398\) immediate descendants, \(27\,547\) of them satisfy the conditions above, and all have \(z
otin D_{c+1}\), by the same exact computation; the descendant step repeated with the corrected ANUPQ gives the same \(27\,547\) presentations. (The nonterminal parents of type \((5,2,1)\) are characterised exactly by Theorem 6.17; this is not needed for Theorem 6.19.) • The group analogue of Theorem C of [IMP26]: is \(D_{2c-1}(G)=1\) for every metabelian group of class \(\le c\)? For \(c=3\) this is Question 1.1. The question reduces to finite metabelian \(p\)-groups (a finite nilpotent quotient is the product of its Sylow subgroups); for \(p\) odd the answer is yes for every \(c\) by [Gup91] (for \(c\le p+1\) already by [GT85, Thm. 3.2]). So only \(p=2\), \(c\ge3\) is open. The plateau group of [IMP26, §3.3] is metabelian of class \(4\) with \(D_6
e1\) (by computation), so \(2c-2\) is attained, as for Lie rings. Its distinguished element \(w\) is not in \(D_7\), and since \(D_6=\langle wangle\) [IMP26], \(D_7=1\) (computed from the dense Howell form modulo \(2^{32}\) of the ideal of relations in the truncated Magnus algebra of rank \(55\,986\), with the exactness certificate): this group is not a counterexample, and the analogue, if true, is sharp at \(c=4\). A first search for a counterexample at \(c=4\) reduces to metabelian quotients of class \(4\) with \(\gamma_4\) finite cyclic, testing its element of order \(2\) (this reduction uses \(D_5^2\subseteq G''\gamma_5\) [MP09, Thm. 2.28] and is proved by hand in the documentation of the code, https://gitlab.com/ispacex/cflint-fast-core, docs/analysis.md, §6.6); about \(170\) such groups (quotients and perturbations of the plateau group, group versions of the Lie ring \(L_1\) of [IMP26, Ex. 3.2], random presentations on \(4\) generators) all have \(D_7\cap\gamma_4=1\) by computation. For \(c=5\), the plateau group shifted up one class (five generators) has \(D_7
e1\) but \(D_8\cap\gamma_5=1\) (by a certified computation), so for metabelian groups of class \(5\) at least \(D_7
e1\) is attained, one short of \(2c-2\); an elementary pairing lemma indicates that the construction would need the exponents of the relations of [IMP26, (3.12)] quadrupled rather than doubled at class \(5\) (the lemma is proved by hand in the same documentation, §6.7), and in our computer experiments with relations modified in this way the distinguished element \(w\) becomes trivial. Code and data: https://gitlab.com/ispacex/cflint-fast-core (docs/analysis.md, §§6.5–6.7).

This is the algebra of Remark 6.4(2). Let \(M=M_1\oplus M_2\oplus M_3\oplus M_4\) over \(\mathbb F_3\) with bases \(M_1=\langle e,k_1,k_2\rangle\), \(M_2=\langle u_1,u_2,\rho\rangle\), \(M_3=\langle t\rangle\), \(M_4=\langle w\rangle\), and the alternating bracket whose nonzero values on pairs of basis elements are, up to antisymmetry, \[\begin{gathered}[e,k_1]=u_1,\quad[e,k_2]=u_2,\quad[k_1,k_2]=\rho,\\ [k_1,u_2]=t,\quad[k_2,u_1]=-t,\quad[e,\rho]=-t,\quad[e,t]=w,\quad[u_1,u_2]=w.\end{gathered}\] It is graded, generated by \(M_1\), of type \((3,3,1,1)\), and \([M_2,M_2]=M_4\ne0\).

Jacobi identity. This is also formally verified, with \([e,\rho]=2t\), which is the same over \(\mathbb F_3\) (§4). The Jacobiator \(J(x,y,z)=[[x,y],z]+[[y,z],x]+[[z,x],y]\) is alternating and trilinear and vanishes in degrees \(\ge5\), so it suffices to check triples of distinct basis elements of total degree \(3\) or \(4\). Degree \(3\): \(J(e,k_1,k_2)=[u_1,k_2]+[\rho,e]+[k_1,u_2]=t+t+t=0\), since \(3=0\) in \(\mathbb F_3\). Degree \(4\), triples \((x,y,z)\) with \(x,y\in M_1\), \(z\in M_2\): as \([k_i,t]=0\) and \([\rho,M_2]=0\), \(J(k_1,k_2,z)=[\rho,z]-[k_1,[k_2,z]]+[k_2,[k_1,z]]=0\) and \(J(e,k_i,z)=[u_i,z]-[e,[k_i,z]]+[k_i,[e,z]]=[u_i,z]-[e,[k_i,z]]\); the last two terms are both \(w\) for \((i,z)=(1,u_2)\), both \(-w\) for \((i,z)=(2,u_1)\), and both \(0\) otherwise. (A machine check of all triples agrees.)

In the notation of the proof of Lemma 6.3, \(\varphi(e)=1\), \(K=\langle k_1,k_2\rangle\), \(u_i=\alpha(e,k_i)\), and \(\alpha(k_1,k_2)=\rho\ne0\) spans the radical of \(\omega\): with \(\dim M_2=3\) the form \(\omega\) may be degenerate, and the step \(\alpha(K,K)=0\) of that proof fails. The Jacobi identity for \((e,k_1,k_2)\), which there gives \(2\,\omega(u_1,u_2)=0\), here reads \(2\,\omega(u_1,u_2)=\beta(e,\rho)\), both sides being \(-1\); with these constants it holds only because \(3t=0\). Taking \([e,\rho]=2t\) instead (the same over \(\mathbb F_3\)) gives such an algebra over \(\mathbb F_p\) for every odd \(p\): then \(J(e,k_1,k_2)=t-2t+t=0\) and both sides above equal \(2\), while the degree-\(4\) triples are unaffected as \([k_i,t]=0\). The Jacobi identity over any commutative ring, and the type and \([M_2,M_2]\ne0\) over any field, are also formally verified (§4); a machine check of all triples for \(p=3,5,7,11\) agrees.
We write out the case \(a=2\), \(x_s^9\in\gamma_3\), of the proof of Theorem 6.8, the only case in which the new terms do not vanish by themselves. The other cases are as in the sketch.

Setting. \(Q\) is a finite \(3\)-group of class \(\le4\), \(Q/\gamma_2\cong C_9\times C_3^{s-1}\) with \(s\ge2\), and \(\gamma_i=\gamma_i(Q)\). Then \(\gamma_3\) is abelian, \(\gamma_4\) is central, \([\gamma_2,\gamma_3]=1\), \([\gamma_2,\gamma_2]\subseteq\gamma_4\), and for \(x\in Q\) the maps \(c\mapsto[c,x]\) and \(c\mapsto[x,c]\) are homomorphisms \(\gamma_3\to\gamma_4\) trivial on \(\gamma_4\).

Identities. (a) \(\gamma_2/\gamma_3\), \(\gamma_3/\gamma_4\) and \(\gamma_4\) are elementary abelian. Indeed, for a basis \(\bar x_1,\dots,\bar x_s\) of \(Q/\gamma_2\) with \(\bar x_s\) of order \(9\), \(\gamma_2/\gamma_3\) is spanned by the \([x_i,x_j]\gamma_3\), \(i<j\), where \(i<s\) and \([x_i,x_j]^3\equiv[x_i^3,x_j]\equiv1\pmod{\gamma_3}\) as \(x_i^3\in\gamma_2\); the other two factors are spanned by the values of bilinear maps whose first argument lies in the previous factor. Hence the proofs of the identities of Theorem 6.6 apply: \(\pi\colon\gamma_2/\gamma_3\to\gamma_3/\gamma_4\), \(a\mapsto a^3\gamma_4\), is a homomorphism and \((ab)^3=a^3b^3\) for \(a,b\in\gamma_2\); and identity (iii) holds for all \(x\in Q\). Moreover, by the Hall–Petrescu formula \((xy)^3\equiv x^3y^3\pmod{\gamma_3}\), so \(x\mapsto x^3\gamma_3\) is a homomorphism \(P\) from \(\Omega=\{x\in Q:x^3\in\gamma_2\}\) to \(\gamma_2/\gamma_3\), trivial on \(\gamma_2\). (b) \([x^9,y]=[x,y]^9\) for all \(x,y\in Q\). Let \(c=[x,y]\). Since \([c,x]\in\gamma_3\) commutes with \(c\) and \([c,x,x]\) is central, \([x^3,y]=c^{x^2}c^xc=c^3f\) with \(f=[c,x]^3[c,x,x]\in\gamma_4\). Put \(Z=x^3\) and \(d=[Z,y]\in\gamma_2\). By (iii), \([d,Z]=[d,x]^3\in\gamma_4\) is central, so \([x^9,y]=[Z^3,y]=d^{Z^2}d^Zd=d^3[d,Z]^3=d^3=c^9f^3=c^9\).

Basis. Let \(W=\Omega/\gamma_2\cong\mathbb F_3^s\), \(\bar P\colon W\to\gamma_2/\gamma_3\) the map induced by \(P\), \(m=\operatorname{rk}\bar P\), and \(\bar z=x_s^3\gamma_2\in W\); then \(\bar P(\bar z)=x_s^9\gamma_3=0\). Choose \(x_1,\dots,x_{s-1}\in\Omega\) such that \(\bar P(\bar x_1),\dots,\bar P(\bar x_m)\) is a basis of \(\operatorname{im}\bar P\) and \(\bar x_{m+1},\dots,\bar x_{s-1},\bar z\) is a basis of \(\ker\bar P\). Then \(\bar x_1,\dots,\bar x_{s-1}\) are independent modulo \(\langle\bar x_s\rangle\cap W=\langle\bar z\rangle\), and \(3^{s-1}\cdot9=|Q/\gamma_2|\), so \(x_1,\dots,x_s\) is a basis of uniqueness of \(Q/\gamma_2\) with \(d(i)=3\) for \(i<s\) and \(d(s)=9\). Put \(Y_i=x_i^3\) for \(i\le m\); these are independent modulo \(\gamma_3\), and we take \(x_{2k}=Y_k\) for \(k\le m\), completed to a basis of \(\gamma_2/\gamma_3\), and all \(e(k)=f(l)=3\) by (a). Then \(b_{ik}=\delta_{ik}\) for \(i\le m\), \(b_{ik}=0\) for \(m<i\le s\) (as \(x_i^3\in\gamma_3\) for \(m<i<s\) and \(x_s^9\in\gamma_3\)), and \(\zeta:=x_s^9\gamma_4=\sum_lc_{sl}\bar x_{3l}\).

Tahara's conditions. By [Tah81, Thm. 6.1], \(D_5(Q)\) is generated by the elements \[g=\sum_{i<j}u_{ij}\tfrac{d(j)}{d(i)}[x_i^{d(i)},x_j]+\sum_{i,k}v_{ik}\sum_{l>k}b_{il}[x_{2l},x_{2k}]+\sum_{i\le j\le k}w_{ijk}[x_i^{d(i)},x_j,x_k]\] over the integer families satisfying (A)–(F) (signs as in the proof of Theorem 6.6). With the orders above we use: (A) \(w_{iii}=0\); (B) for \(i<s\), \(\sum_{i<h\le s}u_{ih}b_{hk}-\sum_{h<i}u_{hi}b_{hk}+3v_{ik}+3v'_{ik}=0\), and for \(i=s\), \(-3\sum_{h<s}u_{hs}b_{hk}+9v_{sk}+3v'_{sk}=0\); (C) \(3\mid u_{ij}\) for \(i<j<s\) (for \(j=s\) it is empty, modulo \(d(i)=3\): in the part of Tahara's (C) with \(\binom{d(i)}3\) and \(\binom{d(i)}2\) the \(u\)-term carries the factor \(d(s)/d(i)=3\) and \(\binom32=3\), and in the part with \(\binom{d(s)}3\) and \(\binom{d(s)}2\), \(3\) divides \(\binom93\) and \(\binom92\)); (D) and (F) exactly as in the proof of Theorem 6.6; and (E), modulo \(3\), \[\sum_kv'_{ik}d_{kl}\equiv\sum_{h>i}u_{ih}c_{hl}-\sum_{h<i}u_{hi}\tfrac{d(i)}{d(h)}\bigl(\alpha^{(hi)}_l+c_{hl}\bigr)-E^w_{il},\] where \(E^w_{il}\) is a sum of products of a coefficient \(w_{\cdots}\) or \(w'_{\cdots}\) with distinguished index \(g\) and some \(\alpha^{(gh)}_l\), \(g\le h\); here \(\alpha^{(gg)}=0\), as read off Tahara's generators of types (V), (VI) [Tah81, pp. 150–151].

\(g=1\) for every admissible family. (1) As in steps (1), (2) of the proof of Theorem 6.6, (D) with \(b_{hk}=\delta_{hk}\) (\(k\le m\)) shows that \(3\) divides every \(w\)-coefficient whose distinguished index is \(\le m\). Hence the \(w\)-part of \(g\) vanishes (for \(i\le m\) by this, for \(m<i<s\) because \(x_i^3\in\gamma_3\), and for \(i=s\) only \(w_{sss}=0\) occurs), and \(E^w_{il}\equiv0\) (for \(g\le m\) by this, for \(m<g<s\) because \([x_g^3,x_h]\in\gamma_4\), and for \(g=s\) because then \(h=s\)). (2) The \(u\)-part. For \(i<j<s\), as in step (3) there, \(u_{ij}[x_i^3,x_j]=u'_{ij}[Y_i,Y_j]\) with \(u_{ij}=3u'_{ij}\), and this is \(1\) unless \(i,j\le m\). For \(j=s\) the term is \([x_i^3,x_s]^{3u_{is}}=[x_i^9,x_s]^{u_{is}}\), since \([x_i^3,x_s]^3=(c^3f)^3=c^9\) in the notation of (b); it is \(1\) for \(m<i<s\), where \(x_i^9\in\gamma_4\). (3) The \(v\)-part is \(\sum_{k<i\le m}v_{ik}[Y_i,Y_k]\). (4) For \(i\le m\), (B) and (F) give, as in step (5) there (the term \(u_{is}b_{sk}\) is \(0\)), \(v'_{ik}=-v_{ik}-U_{ik}\) for \(k\le m\) and \(v'_{ik}=-v_{ik}\) for \(k>m\), with \(U\) the skew matrix \(U_{ik}=u'_{ik}\) (\(i<k\)), and \(v_{kk}\equiv0\), \(v_{lk}\equiv-v_{kl}\) for \(k,l\le m\), \(v_{kl}\equiv0\) for \(k\le m<l\). For \(i=s\), (B) gives \(v'_{sk}=u_{ks}-3v_{sk}\) for \(k\le m\) and \(v'_{sk}=-3v_{sk}\) for \(k>m\). (5) Put \(a_i=\prod_kx_{2k}^{v'_{ik}}\in\gamma_2\), so that the left side of (E) is the coordinate vector of \(\pi(a_i\gamma_3)\). For \(i\le m\) the terms with \(h<i\) vanish modulo \(3\) by (C), and of those with \(h>i\) only \(h=s\) survives; so \(\pi(a_i)=u_{is}\zeta\). For \(i=s\) every \(u\)-term carries the factor \(d(s)/d(h)=3\), so \(\pi(a_s)=0\). Let \(M=v+U\) on indices \(\le m\) (skew with zero diagonal modulo \(3\)), \(r_i=\prod_{k\le m}Y_k^{M_{ik}}\) for \(i\le m\), and \(r_s=\prod_{i\le m}Y_i^{u_{is}}\). By (4), \(a_i\equiv r_i^{-1}\) and \(a_s\equiv r_s\pmod{\gamma_3}\); therefore \[r_i^3\equiv x_s^{-9u_{is}}\pmod{\gamma_4}\quad(i\le m),\qquad r_s^3\in\gamma_4.\] (6) Writing \(\gamma_4\) additively (exponent \(3\), so \(\tfrac12\) makes sense), \[g=\sum_{k<i\le m}M_{ik}[Y_i,Y_k]+\sum_{i\le m}u_{is}[x_i^9,x_s]=\tfrac12\sum_{i\le m}[Y_i,r_i]+\sum_{i\le m}u_{is}[x_i^9,x_s].\] By identity (iii) and (5), \([Y_i,r_i]=[x_i^3,r_i]=[x_i,r_i^3]=[x_i,x_s^9]^{-u_{is}}\), and by (b), \([x_i,x_s^9]=[x_s,x_i]^{-9}=[x_i,x_s]^9=[x_i^9,x_s]\). So, formally, the pairing cancels only half of the new term (in \(\gamma_4\), of exponent \(3\), \(\tfrac12=-1\)): \[g=\bigl(1-\tfrac12\bigr)\sum_{i\le m}u_{is}[x_i^9,x_s]=\tfrac12\Bigl[\prod_{i\le m}x_i^{9u_{is}},\,x_s\Bigr]=\tfrac12\,[r_s^3,x_s],\] since \(x_i^9=Y_i^3\in\gamma_3\) and \(\prod_iY_i^{3u_{is}}=r_s^3\) by (a). By (5), \(r_s^3\in\gamma_4\) is central, so \(g=1\).

The last step is where the row \(s\) of (E) is needed: it sees \(u_{is}\) through \(v'_{sk}\) in (B), where \(d(s)/d(i)=3\). The terms \([x_i^9,x_s]\) need not vanish (see the sketch). The whole computation is also part of the Lean proof of Theorem 6.8 (ExpThreePlus.lean, Setup8.gen_eq_one).

Throughout, \(p\) is odd, \(P\) is as in Theorem 6.17, \(V=P/\gamma_2(P)\cong\mathbb F_p^d\), \([a,b]=a^{-1}b^{-1}ab\), \([a,b,c]=[[a,b],c]\), and \(P_i\) is the lower exponent-\(p\) central series. Lemma. \(P\) is nonterminal if and only if there is a group \(Q\) with a central subgroup \(\langle z\rangle\) of order \(p\) such that \(Q/\langle z\rangle\cong P\) and \(\gamma_4(Q)\ne1\). For every immediate descendant \(Q\) of step size \(1\), \(P_4(Q)=\gamma_4(Q)=\langle z\rangle\), \(\gamma_5(Q)=1\), \(Q''=1\), and \(\gamma_3(Q)\) is elementary abelian of order \(p^2\).

Proof. Let \(Q\) be an immediate descendant of step size \(1\): \(P_4(Q)=\langle z\rangle\) has order \(p\) and \(Q/\langle z\rangle\cong P\). As \(P_3(Q)\) maps onto \(P_3(P)=\gamma_3(P)\), \(P_3(Q)=\gamma_3(Q)\langle z\rangle\) and \(P_4(Q)=\gamma_4(Q)\gamma_3(Q)^p\); also \(\gamma_5(Q)\le P_5(Q)=1\). For \(\ell\in\gamma_2(Q)\) and \(x\in Q\), \([\ell^p,x]=[\ell,x]^p\) since \([\ell,x,\ell]\in\gamma_5(Q)=1\), and \(\ell^p\in P_3(Q)\), so \([\ell,x]^p\in\gamma_4(Q)\). Hence \(\gamma_3(Q)/\gamma_4(Q)\) has exponent \(p\) and \(\langle z\rangle=P_4(Q)=\gamma_4(Q)\). So \(Q\) has class \(4\), its factors \(\gamma_2/\gamma_3\) and \(\gamma_3/\gamma_4\) are those of \(P\), and Lemma 6.3 gives \(Q''=1\). For \(\ell\in\gamma_2(Q)\), \(y\in Q\) and \(c=[\ell,y]\), the element \([c,y]\) is central, so \([\ell,y^p]=c^p[c,y]^{\binom p2}=c^p\); and \(y^p\in\gamma_2(Q)\) (its image lies in \(\gamma_2(P)\), and \(z\in\gamma_2(Q)\)), so \([\ell,y^p]=1\). Since \(\gamma_3(Q)\le\gamma_2(Q)\) is abelian and generated by such \(c\), it has exponent \(p\), and its order is \(p\,|\gamma_3(P)|=p^2\).

Conversely, let \(Q\) be as in the statement. \(\gamma_4(Q)\) maps into \(\gamma_4(P)=1\), so \(\gamma_4(Q)=\langle z\rangle\). The image of \(P_4(Q)\ge\gamma_4(Q)\) in \(P\) is \(P_4(P)=1\), so \(P_4(Q)=\langle z\rangle\) and \(P_5(Q)=[\langle z\rangle,Q]\langle z\rangle^p=1\). As \(z\in\gamma_2(Q)\le\Phi(Q)\), \(d(Q)=d(P)\), so \(Q\) is an immediate descendant of \(P\) [OBr90].

Theorem. Let \(p\) be an odd prime, \(G/\gamma_2(G)\) a finite \(p\)-group and \([\gamma_2(G),\gamma_2(G)]\subseteq\gamma_5(G)\) (e.g. \(G\) metabelian). Then \(D_5(G)=\gamma_5(G)\). In particular \(D_5=\gamma_5\) for finite metabelian \(3\)-groups, which is [GT85, Thm. 3.2(c)] at \(p=3\).

Proof. (The theorem is formally verified, §4, with no restriction on \(\exp(\gamma_2/\gamma_3)\) or on the invariants of \(G/\gamma_2\); at \(p=3\) it removes the hypothesis [GT85] from Lemmas 6.1 and 6.2. For \(p\ge5\) it also follows from [Tah81, Cor. 6.12]. Gupta and Tahara work in the free group ring with Fox derivatives; the route here is Tahara's Theorem 6.1, as for Theorem 6.9.)

Reductions. As for Theorem 6.9, \(\bar G=G/\gamma_5(G)\) is a finite \(p\)-group with \(\gamma_2(\bar G)\) abelian, and it suffices to show \(D_5(Q)=1\) for a finite \(p\)-group \(Q\) with \(\gamma_5=1\) and \(A=\gamma_2(Q)\) abelian.

The module. \(Q\) acts on \(A\) by conjugation, and \(A\) acts trivially, so \(A\), written additively, is a module over the commutative ring \(\mathbb{Z}[Q/\gamma_2]\). With \(t_x=x-1\) we have \([a,x]=a\,t_x\) for \(a\in A\), hence \([a,x,y]=[a,y,x]\), and \(a\,t_xt_yt_z=0\). For \(\theta_{xy}=[x,y]\) (not to be confused with Tahara's constants \(c_{hl}\) below): \([x^n,y]=\theta_{xy}(1+x+\dots+x^{n-1})=\sum_{m\ge1}\binom nm \theta_{xy}t_x^{m-1}\) and \([a,x^n]=n\,a\,t_x+\binom n2a\,t_x^2\).

Lemma 1. If \(x^n\in A\) with \(n\) odd, then \(n\,a\,t_x=0\), i.e. \([a,x]^n=1\), for all \(a\in A\). Indeed \([a,x^n]=1\) as \(A\) is abelian, so \(n\,a\,t_x+\binom n2a\,t_x^2=0\) for all \(a\); for \(a\,t_x\) in place of \(a\) this gives \(n\,a\,t_x^2=0\), hence \(\binom n2a\,t_x^2=\frac{n-1}2\,n\,a\,t_x^2=0\) and \(n\,a\,t_x=0\). Consequently \([x^n,y]=n\,\theta_{xy}+\binom n3\theta_{xy}t_x^2\).

Lemma 2. If \(x^n,y^n\in A\) with \(n\) odd, then \(n\,\theta_{xy}t_z=0\) for all \(z\). Indeed, for \(X=x^n\in A\), \(X\,t_yt_z=X\,t_zt_y\); by Lemma 1 the left side is \(n\,\theta_{xy}t_z\) and the right side \(n\,\theta_{xz}t_y=0\).
